post.title: Composable by Default: How Deco.cx Makes Customization Scalable
post.excerpt: Most CMS platforms give you flexibility or consistency — rarely both. Deco.cx's composable architecture changes that, letting teams move fast without breaking things.

sections.html: There's a classic tension in web platform design. Give teams too much flexibility and you get inconsistent, hard-to-maintain sites. Give them too little and you stifle experimentation. Most platforms resolve this by picking a side — and teams live with the tradeoff.

Deco.cx takes a different approach: composability as the core primitive. Everything is a section. Sections have typed props. Props connect to loaders. Loaders fetch data. The entire architecture is explicit, typed, and composable — which means it scales with your team instead of against it.
"Composable" has become a buzzword, so let's be specific. In Deco.cx, composability means:

sections.items:
Any section can be placed on any page without coupling to that page's data
Sections declare their own data needs via loaders — no prop drilling from parent to child
Apps are self-contained units: they bring their own sections, loaders, and actions
Pages are assembled from sections in Studio, without writing code

sections.html: This means a Hero section built for one campaign can be reused in a product launch without modification. A product carousel can pull from a different data source by swapping its loader. Teams compose experiences the way musicians compose songs — from reusable, interchangeable parts.

Where composability pays off most visibly is in Deco Studio. Editors see the page as a list of sections, each with a form for its props. They can reorder, duplicate, remove, and add sections without touching code. Changes preview instantly. Publish with a click.

sections.quote: Deco Studio gives our team the freedom to experiment without waiting on engineering. We shipped a new landing page variant in two hours — without a single PR.

sections.html: For developers, the Studio experience is a contract: write a section with well-typed props, and non-technical teammates can use it safely. The types you define become the editor's form. No custom CMS schemas to maintain separately from your component props.

Deco.cx ships a library of first-party apps — blog, website, commerce, and more — each providing a set of sections and loaders for a specific domain. Installing a new app is a one-liner in your site's app manifest.

Third-party apps follow the same pattern. The community can publish apps with their own sections, loaders, and UI — and any Deco site can install and compose them in Studio. This is how you get the consistency of a platform with the flexibility of custom development.

The hardest part of web platform design isn't day one — it's month twelve, when the codebase has grown, the team has changed, and you need to make changes without regressions. Composability is the answer: small, well-defined units with clear contracts are easier to understand, test, and replace than large, coupled systems.
Deco.cx sites start composable and stay that way. That's not an accident — it's the architecture.
